project.title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Factual Question Answering over a University Policy Corpus
project.research_question: RQ1: Does retrieval-augmented generation improve factual question answering accuracy over closed-book models on university policy documents? RQ2: Does passage retrieval reduce unsupported claims?
objectives: Evaluate answer correctness on 120 benchmark questions
Quantify reduction in unsupported factual claims
Perform paired significance testing via McNemar test
project.claimed_contribution: A paired evaluation framework establishing that retrieval augmentation improves accuracy from 59.2% to 81.7% with p = 0.0000143.
project.methodology: We employ a within-question paired design using 120 benchmark questions, evenly distributed across academic regulations, course registration, financial assistance, and campus services. Each question was processed by the ResearchBuddy-Sim-7B-Instruct v1.0 model in two conditions: (1) Closed-book, and (2) RAG with top-5 passages retrieved via Embed-Sim-v1. Evaluation performed via human-style annotation with synthetic Cohen's kappa of 0.82. Paired discordant pairs evaluated using exact two-sided McNemar test.
project.dataset_or_materials: 120 curated university policy questions paired with official institutional documentation passages.
project.results: In the primary evaluation of answer-level correctness, the closed-book condition resulted in 71 correct answers (59.2%), while the RAG condition resulted in 98 correct answers (81.7%). The paired contingency table reveals that 65 questions were correct in both, 33 were correct only in RAG, 6 were correct only in closed-book, and 16 were incorrect in both. An exact two-sided McNemar test on the discordant pairs (33 vs 6) yields p = 0.0000143, indicating statistical significance. Unsupported claims fell from 52 of 120 (43.3%) to 24 of 120 (20.0%).
project.limitations: The findings are derived from synthetic data, a single model architecture, and a simplified retrieval pipeline.

cases.source_draft: We evaluated 120 questions across university policy domains. Closed-book got 71 correct (59.2%), RAG got 98 correct (81.7%). Contingency: 65 both correct, 33 RAG only, 6 closed only, 16 neither. McNemar p = 0.0000143. Unsupported claims: 52 (43.3%) closed-book down to 24 (20.0%) RAG. Cohen's kappa was 0.82.

references.text: Lewis, P., et al. (2020). Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. NeurIPS.
Karpukhin, V., et al. (2020). Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering. EMNLP.

project.title: Adaptive Hierarchical Routing for Distributed Edge Model Inference
project.research_question: How can dynamic priority queuing optimize tail latency in multi-tenant edge inferencing without violating strict memory budgets?
objectives: Formulate analytical queuing dynamics under Lyapunov drift optimization
Characterize theoretical memory bounds under heterogeneous packet arrivals
project.claimed_contribution: A theoretical routing framework with proven upper bounds on queue backlog and latency.
project.methodology: We formulate an analytical queuing model using Markov decision processes and Lyapunov drift optimization across 3 edge topologies. State space transitions are bounded by Lipschitz continuity over arrival distributions.
project.limitations: Theoretical formulation has not been deployed on physical hardware.

cases.source_draft: This paper presents a theoretical formulation of adaptive hierarchical routing for distributed edge inference. Physical experiments have not been conducted.

references.text: Neely, M. J. (2010). Stochastic Network Optimization with Application to Communication and Queueing Systems. Morgan & Claypool.

project.title: A Systematic Comparative Analysis of Neural and Sparse Information Retrieval Paradigms
project.research_question: How do sparse inverted index mechanisms compare against dense dual-encoder embeddings across high-stakes factual retrieval benchmarks?
objectives: Thematically categorize sparse, dense, and learned lexical retrieval architectures
Contrast memory footprint, latency, and out-of-domain robustness
project.claimed_contribution: A comprehensive comparative synthesis establishing trade-off surfaces between dense and sparse retrieval paradigms.
project.methodology: A comparative meta-synthesis evaluating algorithmic complexity, index storage footprint, and out-of-domain robustness across standardized literature benchmarks.
project.limitations: Synthesizes published literature and does not conduct independent cluster-scale re-indexing.

cases.source_draft: A comprehensive conceptual comparison between sparse retrieval (BM25, SPLADE) and dense retrieval (DPR).

project.title: Cross-Attention Gating for Multimodal Histopathology Classification and Patient Survival Stratification
project.research_question: Does cross-attention gating between gigapixel whole-slide histology and genomic profiles improve patient survival stratification over unimodal baselines?
objectives: Design a weakly supervised cross-attention gating pipeline
Evaluate Concordance Index on a 500-patient multi-center cohort
Validate statistical significance using paired two-sided t-tests
project.claimed_contribution: A multimodal gating architecture achieving a C-Index of 0.732 over unimodal baselines with p = 0.0021.
project.methodology: We curate a multi-center cohort of 500 patient biopsies. Whole-slide images are tiled into 256x256 patches and encoded using a ResNet-50 backbone. Genomic features are projected via dense multi-layer perceptrons into a shared latent space. Cross-attention gating decouples modality-specific noise. Survival analysis is evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression with 5-fold cross-validation.
project.dataset_or_materials: 500 patient biopsies with matched whole-slide images and RNA sequencing profiles.
project.results: Across 5-fold cross-validation on the 500-patient cohort, the proposed cross-attention model achieved a Concordance Index (C-Index) of 0.732 (95% CI: 0.695-0.769), outperforming genomics alone (0.648) and histology alone (0.671). The paired t-test confirmed statistical significance (p = 0.0021).
project.limitations: Evaluated on retrospective cohorts; requires prospective clinical trial validation.

cases.source_draft: 500-patient cohort evaluated. Multimodal C-Index was 0.732 vs 0.648 (genomics) and 0.671 (histology). Paired t-test p = 0.0021. Retrospective cohort limitations.

references.text: Lu, M. Y., et al. (2021). AI-based pathology predicts origins for cancers of unknown primary. Nature.
Chen, R. J., et al. (2022). Multimodal co-attention transformer for survival prediction. Nature Biomedical Engineering.
